1. Meaning of Panchayati Raj

  • Panchayati Raj is the system of Rural Local Self-Government through democratically elected institutions.

It functions at:

  • Village level.
  • Intermediate level.
  • District level.

It enables rural people to participate directly in:

  • Local administration.
  • Development planning.
  • Decision-making.
  • Implementation of welfare programmes.
  • Panchayati Raj represents the third tier of Government in rural India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panchayati Raj → Rural Local Self-Government

2. Meaning of Panchayat

The word Panchayat is derived from:

  • “Panch” → Five.
  • Traditionally, village affairs were managed by councils of respected elders.
  • Modern Panchayats are constitutional institutions of democratic self-government.

3. Objectives of Panchayati Raj

Panchayati Raj seeks to promote:

  • Democratic decentralisation.
  • People's participation.
  • Rural development.
  • Social justice.
  • Local planning.
  • Better public-service delivery.
  • Grassroots democracy.
  • Local accountability.

4. Democratic Decentralisation

Democratic decentralisation involves transfer of:

  • Powers.
  • Functions.
  • Funds.
  • Functionaries

from higher levels of Government to elected Local Bodies.

📌 Must-Memorise

Effective Panchayati Raj → Powers + Functions + Funds + Functionaries

5. Constitutional Framework

Panchayati Raj is governed by:

  • Part IX.
  • Articles 243–243O.
  • Eleventh Schedule.

These provisions were inserted by:

  • 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.

The Amendment came into force on:

  • 24 April 1993.
📌 Must-Memorise

73rd Amendment → Part IX + Articles 243–243O + Eleventh Schedule

6. National Panchayati Raj Day

The 73rd Constitutional Amendment came into force on:

  • 24 April 1993.

The date is observed as:

  • National Panchayati Raj Day.
📌 Must-Memorise

24 April → National Panchayati Raj Day

Local Government is included in:

  • Entry 5 of State List.
  • Seventh Schedule.

State Legislatures enact laws relating to:

within the constitutional framework.

8. Ancient Village Self-Government

Ancient Indian villages possessed institutions relating to:

  • Village assemblies.
  • Community decision-making.
  • Local dispute resolution.
  • Common-resource management.
  • Collective responsibility.
  • Local administration.

9. Medieval Village Panchayats

During the medieval period, village Panchayats continued performing functions involving:

  • Local administration.
  • Dispute settlement.
  • Revenue collection.
  • Maintenance of public works.
  • Their powers varied among different kingdoms.

10. Panchayats under British Rule

  • British administration was initially highly centralised.
  • Traditional village institutions gradually weakened.

Later colonial reforms encouraged:

  • Local administration.
  • Financial decentralisation.
  • Local representation.

11. Lord Mayo's Resolution, 1870

Lord Mayo's Resolution encouraged:

  • Financial decentralisation.
  • Greater local administrative responsibility.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lord Mayo → 1870 → Financial Decentralisation

12. Lord Ripon's Resolution, 1882

Lord Ripon is known as:

  • Father of Local Self-Government in India.

His Resolution promoted:

  • Elected Local Bodies.
  • Non-official participation.
  • Administrative decentralisation.
  • Local financial responsibility.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lord Ripon → 1882 → Father of Local Self-Government

13. Royal Commission on Decentralisation, 1907

The Commission recommended strengthening:

  • Village Panchayats.
  • Local administration.
  • Decentralised governance.

14. Government of India Act, 1919

Local Self-Government became a transferred subject under:

  • Dyarchy.
  • Indian Ministers in Provinces received greater responsibility for local administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

1919 Act → Local Self-Government → Transferred Subject

15. Government of India Act, 1935

The Act increased:

  • Provincial autonomy.
  • Provincial responsibility over Local Government.

16. Article 40

  • The original Constitution did not grant constitutional status to Panchayats.

Article 40 in the Directive Principles directs the State to:

  • Organise Village Panchayats.
  • Endow them with necessary powers.
  • Enable them to function as Units of Self-Government.
  • Article 40 is non-justiciable.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 40 → Organisation of Village Panchayats

17. Community Development Programme, 1952

The Community Development Programme was launched in:

  • 1952.

Its objectives included:

  • Agricultural development.
  • Rural infrastructure.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Public participation remained limited.

18. National Extension Service, 1953

The National Extension Service was launched in:

  • 1953.

Its aims included:

  • Expansion of rural development.
  • Wider administrative outreach.
  • Better implementation of development programmes.

19. Need for Stronger Panchayati Raj

Problems before constitutional reform included:

  • Centralised administration.
  • Weak village participation.
  • Irregular elections.
  • Poor financial resources.
  • Limited powers.
  • Lack of constitutional protection.
  • Uneven development among States.

The Committee was appointed in:

  • 1957.

It examined:

The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended:

  • Democratic Decentralisation.
  • Establishment of Panchayati Raj Institutions.

The Committee recommended:

  • Gram Panchayat → Village.
  • Panchayat Samiti → Block.
  • Zila Parishad → District.
📌 Must-Memorise

Balwant Rai Mehta → Three-Tier Panchayati Raj

23. Gram Panchayat under Balwant Rai Mehta

The Gram Panchayat was recommended to be:

  • Directly elected.
  • Responsible for local administration.

24. Panchayat Samiti under Balwant Rai Mehta

The Committee regarded Panchayat Samiti as:

  • Executive authority of Panchayati Raj.
  • Most important unit of planning and development at the Block level.

25. Zila Parishad under Balwant Rai Mehta

The Zila Parishad was expected to:

  • Coordinate development programmes.
  • Supervise Panchayat Samitis.

26. Other Balwant Rai Mehta Recommendations

  • Financial decentralisation.
  • People's participation.
  • Democratic elections.
  • Administrative decentralisation.

41. Constitutional Status in 1992

  • Panchayats previously functioned mainly as statutory bodies under State laws.
  • The 73rd Constitutional Amendment transformed them into constitutionally recognised Institutions of Self-Government.

42. Main Features of the 73rd Amendment

The Amendment introduced:

  • Constitutional status.
  • Gram Sabha.
  • Three-tier system.
  • Direct elections.
  • Reservation.
  • Five-year tenure.
  • State Election Commission.
  • State Finance Commission.
  • Eleventh Schedule.
  • Constitutional safeguards.

43. Article 243

  • Article 243 contains definitions used in Part IX.

It covers terms such as:

  • District.
  • Gram Sabha.
  • Intermediate Level.
  • Panchayat.
  • Panchayat Area.
  • Population.
  • Village.

44. Article 243A

Article 243A deals with:

  • Gram Sabha.

Gram Sabha exercises powers and functions provided by:

  • State Legislature through law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243A → Gram Sabha

45. Meaning of Gram Sabha

Gram Sabha is:

  • General Assembly of all registered voters

living within the area of a Village Panchayat.

46. Gram Sabha Membership

Membership is automatic for:

  • Every registered voter whose name appears in the village electoral roll.
  • No separate election is required for Gram Sabha membership.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Gram Sabha → All Registered Voters → No Election for Membership

47. Gram Sabha as Direct Democracy

Gram Sabha represents:

  • Direct Democracy

at village level.

It enables people to participate in:

  • Development planning.
  • Monitoring.
  • Social audit.
  • Accountability.
  • Local decision-making.

48. Gram Sabha Functions

Depending on State law, Gram Sabha may:

  • Approve village development plans.
  • Identify scheme beneficiaries.
  • Review Panchayat accounts.
  • Examine use of public funds.
  • Monitor welfare programmes.
  • Conduct social audits.
  • Discuss development issues.

49. Gram Sabha Meetings

Frequency of Gram Sabha meetings is determined by:

  • State Panchayat Acts.
  • Constitution does not prescribe a uniform number of meetings.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Gram Sabha Meeting Frequency → State Law, Not Fixed by Constitution

50. Gram Sabha vs Gram Panchayat

Gram Sabha:

  • All registered voters.
  • Direct democracy.
  • Permanent general body.
  • Reviews and monitors development.

Gram Panchayat:

  • Elected body.
  • Representative democracy.
  • Implements schemes.
  • Performs village administration.

51. Article 243B

Article 243B provides for Panchayats at:

  • Village level.
  • Intermediate level.
  • District level.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243B → Three Levels of Panchayats

52. Three-Tier System

The three levels are:

  • Gram Panchayat → Village.
  • Panchayat Samiti → Intermediate / Block / Taluk / Mandal.
  • Zila Parishad → District.

53. Population Exception

States with population below:

  • 20 lakh

are not constitutionally required to establish:

  • Intermediate-level Panchayat.
📌 Must-Memorise

Below 20 Lakh Population → Intermediate Tier Not Mandatory

54. Gram Panchayat

Gram Panchayat is the:

  • Basic unit of Rural Local Government.

It functions at:

  • Village level.
  • It performs executive and development functions at village level.

55. Gram Panchayat Composition

It generally includes:

  • Directly elected ward members.
  • Sarpanch or President.
  • Deputy Sarpanch, where provided.
  • Exact composition is determined by State law.

56. Head of Gram Panchayat

The head may be called:

  • Sarpanch.
  • President.
  • Panchayat President.

depending on State law.

57. Gram Panchayat Functions

Common functions include:

  • Drinking water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Village roads.
  • Street lighting.
  • Rural housing.
  • Public health.
  • Welfare schemes.
  • Agriculture.
  • Rural development.
  • Community assets.

58. Panchayat Samiti

Panchayat Samiti functions at:

  • Intermediate level.

It may operate at:

  • Block.
  • Taluk.
  • Mandal level.

It links:

  • Gram Panchayat.
  • Zila Parishad.

59. Panchayat Samiti Functions

It generally:

  • Coordinates village development.
  • Supervises Gram Panchayats.
  • Implements Block-level programmes.
  • Provides technical assistance.
  • Monitors Government schemes.

60. Zila Parishad

Zila Parishad is:

  • Highest tier of Panchayati Raj.

It functions at:

  • District level.

61. Zila Parishad Functions

Zila Parishad commonly performs:

  • District development planning.
  • Coordination of Panchayat Samitis.
  • Allocation of development funds.
  • Supervision of rural programmes.
  • Monitoring Government schemes.

62. Functional Relationship of Three Tiers

Gram Panchayat:

  • Village administration.
  • Local implementation.

Panchayat Samiti:

  • Block coordination.
  • Technical supervision.

Zila Parishad:

  • District planning.
  • Overall coordination and supervision.

64. Territorial Constituencies

Panchayat areas are divided into:

  • Territorial Constituencies or Wards.
  • Members are directly elected from these constituencies.

65. Direct Election

Members of Panchayats are:

  • Directly elected by people from territorial constituencies.

Panchayat Members → Direct Election

66. Election of Chairpersons

Method of electing Panchayat Chairpersons is determined by:

  • State Legislature.

Depending on State law, the Chairperson may be:

  • Directly elected.
  • Indirectly elected.

67. Representation of MPs and MLAs

State law may provide representation at intermediate and district levels for:

  • Members of Parliament.
  • Members of State Legislature.
  • Voting rights depend on State legislation.

68. Article 243D

Article 243D provides reservation for:

  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
  • Women.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243D → Reservation in Panchayats

69. SC and ST Reservation

Seats for SCs and STs are reserved:

  • Broadly in proportion to their population in the Panchayat area.

70. Reservation for Women

Not less than:

  • One-third of total seats

must be reserved for women.

This includes:

  • SC women.
  • ST women.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panchayat Women Reservation → Minimum 1/3

71. Chairperson Reservation for Women

Not less than one-third of Chairperson offices at Panchayat levels must be reserved for:

  • Women.
  • States may provide higher reservation.

72. Reservation by Rotation

Reserved seats may be allotted by:

  • Rotation

as provided by State law.

73. Backward Class Reservation

State Legislatures may provide reservation for:

  • Backward Classes.

Extent and method depend on:

  • State law.
  • Constitutional principles.
  • Judicial decisions.

74. Article 243E

Article 243E deals with:

  • Duration of Panchayats.

Normal tenure:

  • Five years from date appointed for first meeting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243E → Panchayat Tenure → 5 Years

75. Election Before Expiry

Fresh Panchayat elections must be completed:

  • Before expiry of existing five-year term.

76. Election after Dissolution

If Panchayat is dissolved early:

  • Election must ordinarily be held within six months.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panchayat Dissolution → Election within 6 Months

77. Less-than-Six-Month Exception

If remaining term is:

  • Less than six months,

fresh election need not be held merely for that short remainder.

78. Term of Reconstituted Panchayat

A Panchayat elected after premature dissolution ordinarily serves:

  • Only the remaining period of the original five-year term.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Reconstituted Panchayat → Remainder of Original Term

79. Article 243F

Article 243F deals with:

  • Disqualifications for Panchayat membership.

80. Minimum Age

A person who has completed:

  • 21 years

cannot be disqualified merely because he or she has not completed 25 years.

General minimum age for Panchayat membership is therefore:

  • 21 years

subject to applicable law.

📌 Must-Memorise

Panchayat Election Minimum Age → 21 Years

81. Panchayat Disqualifications

Possible grounds include:

  • Office of Profit.
  • Unsound mind declared by competent court.
  • Undischarged insolvency.
  • Loss of citizenship.
  • Corrupt electoral practices.
  • State-law disqualification.
  • Other statutory grounds.

82. Authority Deciding Disqualification

Questions relating to disqualification are determined by:

  • Authority prescribed by State law.

83. Article 243G

Article 243G deals with:

  • Powers.
  • Authority.
  • Responsibilities of Panchayats.

  • Institutions of Self-Government.
